title: Bridging the Cultural Context Gap in Global E-commerce
summary: Aesop’s brand is built on a "less is more" philosophy. However, global performance data revealed a major friction point: users were dropping off at the very first step of the checkout journey. Surprisingly, Japan had the highest drop-off rates globally. The challenge was to diagnose why a minimalist interface—which traditionally reduces friction—was actually causing it in certain high-value markets.

tabs.label: Challenge
tabs.subtitle: Aesop's global checkout was performing exactly as designed: clean, minimal, frictionless. Except in Japan, where 52% of users abandoned at the first step—nearly double the rate of any other market.

tabs.label: Approach
tabs.body:
Information architecture gap: Progressive disclosure hid gift wrapping and sample offerings—critical to Japanese purchasing decisions—until Step 3. Users arriving at checkout interpreted absence of visible gifting services as unavailability.
Wayfinding deficit: Isolated step progression created perceived uncertainty about checkout length and stage completion, violating basic task-completion heuristics.
tabs.subtitle: Analysis of qualitative feedback (on-site surveys, regional stakeholder interviews) revealed a structural mismatch between interface philosophy and cultural expectations:

tabs.body:
Design for trust, not mystery — Provide reassurance at the moment it's needed, not after hesitation has already set in
Service is a conversion driver — Gifting, sustainability, delivery clarity, and customer care are not secondary; they justify the purchase
Orientation reduces effort — A clearly mapped journey feels shorter than an abstract one, even if the number of steps stays the same
